newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil eases as Iraqi oil continues to weigh.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil eases as Iraqi oil continues to weigh.

text.p: World oil prices were slightly easier on Thursday as downward pressure from looming Iraqi oil exports more than offset strong underlying demand.
Iraq is preparing to resume oil exports under an oil-for-food exchange with the United Nations but traders said underlying demand for oil was strong and any price weakness may prove temporary.
Oil companies were jostling for position on Thursday to rent tankers after Wednesday's news that United Nations oil experts or overseers had approved Iraq's pricing formula for its oil.
That was nearly the final go ahead for Iraq to sell oil. The pricing formula was passed to the U.N. sanctions committee which has until 1500 GMT Friday to raise any objections.
Otherwise the formula is accepted and Iraq can sell oil which trades said may hit the market within a few days.
But Iraqi appeared to adding a political twist to the oil sales on Thursday.
Baghdad snubbed requests from British Petroleum and Shell to buy oil but French company Elf said it expected to renew it's contract from the previous oil-for-food deal.
Iraqi's oil minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed said on Wednesday that Iraqi would give "priority" to companies and states that adopted a "positive" stance towards Iraq.
London September North Sea Brent blend futures were down two cents at $19.19 a barrel at 1508 GMT.
Despite downward pressure from the imminent flood of Iraqi oil some dealers expected only a modest and short-lived drop in oil prices.
They said demand to restock ahead of the winter was likely to boost demand over the next few months and the delay in Iraq resuming oil exports had crimped the normal summer stockbuild.
Sales under the second phase of Iraq's oil-for-food exchange with the U.N. were delayed since early June by negotiations over an aid distribution plan.
But Iraq is now expected to move full steam ahead in an effort to meet its permitted $2.14 billion worth of sales, including $140 million for Turkish pipeline fees, in two equal 90-day instalments.
It will have less than a month to reach an initial billion dollar target by September 5 which implies a flood of early cargoes.
But after that date exports are likely to reigned back to a level which traders can easily be absorbed by the market.
"I see the chance of one last down move when gasoline falls followed by a quick move back up," said a trader.
Gasoline prices have rallied recently in the West but with the summer driving season all but over demand is on the wane.
